title: p99/p95 tail latency deep dive with Helio Robotics
next_steps: Run 24h p95/p99 benchmark with Helio's traffic profile (Redwood/Helio) - due 2027-09-15
Share latency playbook and KV cache tuning doc (Redwood) - due 2027-09-10

action_items: Samir: Share pricing/commit options and Dedicated capacity notes (due 2027-09-10)
Olivia: Produce benchmark template and test script for p95/p99 runs (due 2027-09-14)
Maya: Provide Helio production traffic sample and SLOs (due 2027-09-12)
transcript:
[00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm samir from Redwood Inference. quick roll call?
[00:12] Evan - Helio (Eng Manager): hey evan here, maya's on the call too, liam and priya also joined.
[00:20] Samir: awesome, goal for today is a technical deep dive on p95/p99 tail latency — streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache behavior, batching, quantization and network hops. we want to understand your production profile and see where we can optimise.
[00:35] Maya - Helio (SRE): great, our main pain is sporadic p99 spikes during peak hours, sometimes 2-3x above p95 and it kills our SLAs.
[00:46] Olivia (Redwood SE): got it. quick question: are you doing streaming responses today or waiting for full non-streamed payloads?
[00:52] Liam - Helio (ML Infra): mostly non-streaming right now. we switched to streaming for chat but our customer-facing inference is non-streamed batch requests.
[01:05] Jordan (Redwood SE): and what model sizes are you serving?
[01:09] Evan: 13B and a couple of 70B variants for higher fidelity tasks. both are quantized to 4-bit in our infra.
[01:18] Olivia: ok that helps. key knobs we'll discuss: KV cache hit rates and cache locality, batching strategy and max batch latency, quantization profile tradeoffs, and network hop contributions (LB -> control plane -> GPU node -> storage).
[01:33] Maya: for KV cache, we saw hit rates around 45% which seems low — our prompts often have long prefixes but users vary.
[01:42] Samir: 45% is tough; Redwood's prefix caching can push that higher with per-route cache keys and smarter TTLs. there might be tokenization differences causing misses, e.g., whitespace or user id in the prompt.
[01:57] Evan: yeah we do inject session metadata, might be low locality because of that.
[02:05] Olivia: quick primer: p95 measures typical high latency but p99 is tail — often dominated by cold KV cache misses, straggler batches, or network retries.
[02:16] Maya: curious — which of those usually dominates in Redwood's hosted env?
[02:20] Olivia: in hosted we frequently see two classes: 1) kernel warmup/cold attention cache on GPU (first few requests after a scale-out) and 2) KV cache misses that require recompute. network hops are smaller but non-zero — ~2-8ms extra per cross-az hop.
[02:36] Jordan: adding to that, batching behavior matters — if you set a max batching latency of 20ms you'll reduce GPU idle but can increase tail if a straggler keeps a batch waiting.
[02:48] Priya - Helio (Security): quick security Q: for Dedicated/VPC, is the KV cache stored on customer nodes or in Redwood-managed memory?
[02:56] Samir: in Dedicated/VPC deployments the KV cache resides on the customer's GPU nodes and is managed locally; keys and artifacts never leave the VPC. for hosted tenants it's in our serving layer but encrypted at rest and in transit, with K-M-S integration. (note: transcript sometimes says K-M-S as KMS).
[03:15] Maya: good. we want to keep data in-house for compliance.
[03:19] Olivia: then Dedicated or Private is better — that removes cross-tenant noisy neighbors for memory pressure and also reduces network overlay hops which helps tail.
[03:27] Evan: can you walk through a p99 scenario step-by-step?
[03:31] Olivia: sure. imagine a user request that hits a cold worker (no KV cache) -> scheduler queues batch -> batch sent to GPU -> model does attention and fills KV cache -> response returned. p99 gets hit if any of these steps spike: cold worker warmup (compilation/kernels), scheduler delay because of bursty traffic or retry/backpressure, or a cache miss results in full forward instead of cached prefix. also if you're non-streaming and waiting for the whole output, you add generation time on top.
[03:58] Liam: do kernel warmups still happen with the newer JIT/kernels?
[04:02] Olivia: less than before but yes — model variants, sequence length, and quantization path can trigger different kernels. compiling kernels or choosing a slower fallback kernel can add tens to hundreds of ms.
[04:15] Maya: what about quantization? our 4-bit runs are cheaper but maybe worse p99?
[04:20] Jordan: there's a tradeoff: aggressive quantization can increase compute time per token if it forces a suboptimal kernel or more frequent dequant/dequantize ops; conversely, smaller memory footprint can reduce IO and improve throughput. it's workload dependent.
[04:36] Evan: so we should test both 4-bit and 8-bit variants under our traffic.
[04:40] Olivia: exactly. our Redwood Optimize tool suggests quant profiles based on token mix and priority of latency vs cost — we'll share that report.
[04:49] [05:00] Speaker 1: there's a bit of crosstalk — sorry, go ahead.
[05:05] Samir: let's pivot to network hops. Maya, are your nodes spread across AZs?
[05:10] Maya: yes, multi-AZ for resilience.
[05:13] Olivia: cross-AZ can add 3-12ms per hop. for p99 tight SLOs we recommend pinning traffic to AZ-local pools or using regional dedicated nodes for consistency.
[05:25] Evan: what about streaming vs non-streaming — does streaming help tail latency?
[05:30] Olivia: streaming hides generation latency to clients because you start sending tokens earlier, so perceived p99 for first-byte is lower. but if you measure end-to-end completion time p99 for total generation can remain high. streaming also interacts with batching differently — partial batches can be flushed earlier.
[05:47] Liam: interesting. most of our observability measures completion time, not first-byte.
[05:51] Jordan: we can instrument both metrics. first-byte p95/p99 and completion p95/p99.
[05:57] Maya: about batching, we're using a fixed max batch size of 32 with a batching delay of 15ms.
[06:04] Olivia: 15ms is aggressive — it gives good throughput but can create stragglers if traffic variance is high. consider adaptive batching: size cap + latency cap + priority routes for low-latency calls.
[06:17] Samir: Redwood's runtime supports workload-aware batching and can do per-route overrides so you can keep important routes low-latency while letting less-critical routes batch more.
[06:26] Evan: how do we measure KV cache locality?
[06:29] Olivia: we instrument hits/misses per route, per session key. we'll need your traffic sample to compute effective cache hit rate for the actual prefix distributions.
[06:37] Maya: i'll upload a 24h sample of anonymized prompts.
[06:41] Priya: note — data must be scrubbed of PII before sharing.
[06:44] Samir: absolutely, scrubbed is fine; we'll accept hashed session ids.
[06:49] [07:00] Olivia: another vector: we saw customers with long prompt prefixes with low variance do very well with a prefix-based hotcache; if your prefixes vary with user id injects, consider moving user-specific metadata to a separate param so cache keys are stable.
[07:16] Liam: can you give an example?
[07:18] Olivia: instead of embedding "User: 12345" in the prompt body, pass it as a metadata token not included in prefix hashing. small dev change, big cache effect.
[07:29] Evan: ok noted.
[07:33] Maya: what's the cost of keeping larger KV caches on GPU memory? we have limited memory per GPU.
[07:40] Jordan: larger KV caches increase memory footprint but reduce recompute. it's a trade: use more memory per worker or accept more compute and latency. also sharded KV caches across GPUs can complicate network traffic if not colocated.
[07:55] Olivia: for Dedicated deployments we often provision slightly larger GPU memory per worker or use denser GPUs to host bigger caches, which reduces p99.
[08:05] Evan: what about autoscaling — does scale-out cause p99 blips?
[08:09] Olivia: yes, scale-out introduces cold workers; we mitigate with warm pools and predictive scaling. Redwood can keep a minimum pool to avoid cold starts during known peak windows.
[08:19] Maya: can warm pools be in a different AZ?
[08:22] Samir: we recommend keeping warm pools AZ-local to avoid cross-AZ latency.
[08:27] [08:30] Priya: security question — for Private on-prem, do you need any inbound from our network to Redwood?
[08:35] Samir: for Private control plane you do a webhook to notify status but no inference data leaves your network; we can run fully air-gapped deployments with a managed upgrade channel.
[08:45] Priya: ok thanks.
[08:48] Olivia: next, retries and backpressure — misconfigured retries can amplify spikes: if clients retry on 5xx quickly you create batch queuing and higher p99 across the board.
[08:58] Liam: we saw a retry storm once — that was painful. any best practice?
[09:02] Jordan: exponential backoff + jitter, surface 429 for overloaded endpoints, and per-route circuit breakers.
[09:10] Evan: any quick wins we can try this week?
[09:13] Olivia: yes: 1) run 1h small-scale benchmark reproducing peak qps to identify straggler sources, 2) increase KV cache TTL for hot prefixes, 3) reduce cross-AZ routing for latency-critical paths, 4) instrument first-byte vs completion metrics.
[09:29] Maya: we can start with those.
[09:32] Samir: we'll share a benchmark template and the Redwood latency playbook link: https://redwood.example.com/latency-playbook (this is a reference link).
[09:44] [10:00] Speaker 1: minor audio glitch.
[10:05] Olivia: about quantization testing — we recommend side-by-side runs with the same traffic to compare latency and quality. Redwood Optimize can run A/B runs and provide a recommendation.
[10:18] Evan: curious — do you do KV cache serialization between model variants? e.g., 13B and 70B caches incompatible?
[10:25] Olivia: typically KV cache is model-architecture dependent. kernels and layouts differ; you shouldn't share caches across different families. we do support warm-starting by rerunning prefixes on target model though.
[10:39] Liam: got it.
[10:42] Maya: earlier you mentioned scheduler delays — can you explain Redwood's scheduling policy?
[10:47] Jordan: scheduler is priority aware, we use continuous batching with timeout thresholds. small latency-critical requests can be prioritized and flushed early; larger batchable requests wait to fill. we also do pressure-aware shedding to avoid queue explosion.
[11:02] Priya: any secrets in the scheduler we should be aware of?
[11:05] Samir: nothing secret — it's configurable per-tenant with defaults tuned for low p99 and cost.
[11:13] Evan: what's a typical p99 improvement customers see after KV cache and batching tuning?
[11:18] Olivia: customers often see 30-60% p99 improvement for prefix-heavy workloads, sometimes more if the initial architecture was putting user ids in prompts.
[11:28] Maya: that's promising.
[11:31] [12:00] Olivia: for benchmarking, we'll need: anonymized 24h traffic sample (Maya), target SLOs (Evan), and preferred model/quant configs (Liam). we'll supply a benchmark script and sample infra config for Dedicated or Private.
[12:47] Samir: now let's discuss instrumentation — what metrics do you currently collect?
[12:51] Evan: we track latency histograms, p50/p95/p99, error rates, and token counts; but not first-byte separately.
[12:59] Olivia: add kernel selection metrics, KV cache hit/miss per-route, batch sizes distribution, and cross-AZ latency tags. those help root cause tail events.
[13:12] Maya: can Redwood push those traces into our Datadog?
[13:16] Jordan: yes, we have tracing hooks and can send metrics/logs to Datadog, Prometheus, or your SIEM.
[13:24] Priya: we'll want audit logs for model access.
[13:27] Samir: audit logs are available in Dedicated/Private with retention controls.
[13:31] Olivia: quick note on streaming: we can stream generation as tokens become available or buffer to send in micro-chunks; micro-chunking reduces first-byte latency while keeping batching efficiency.
[13:43] Evan: curious about the micro-chunk tuning — is that automatic?
[13:46] Olivia: we can enable auto-flush thresholds by token count or time; it's another knob to tune.
[13:54] Liam: let's talk numbers — currently our p95 is 180ms and p99 is 620ms for completion time at peak.
[14:03] Samir: what's your target?
[14:05] Evan: we'd like p95 < 150ms and p99 < 300ms for our main route.
[14:11] Olivia: achievable but will require: better KV hit rates (target >70%), AZ-local pools, adaptive batching, and possibly switching the hot route to streaming or micro-chunks.
[14:23] Maya: what kind of hardware changes might help?
[14:26] Olivia: denser GPUs with larger memory reduce cache eviction; NVLink within nodes reduces KV sync times; faster NVMe for swap/overflow can help but is slower than GPU mem.
[14:38] Evan: cost-wise what's the delta?
[14:41] Samir: Dedicated with denser GPUs is more expensive but predictable. Redwood Optimize can model cost per token vs latency benefit so you can decide.
[14:51] [15:00] Speaker 1: small echo.
[15:04] Olivia: about retries — one pattern we recommend is to return 202 or 429 for heavy load and let clients degrade gracefully; also surface a retry-after header.
[15:17] Liam: ok we'll adjust clients.
[15:21] Maya: to validate our assumptions, can Redwood run a simulated run at our scale?
[15:25] Olivia: yes, Redwood can run a dedicated benchmark cluster with your traffic profile to reproduce tail behaviors — we'll need the sample and a time window.
[15:35] Samir: we'll set up the benchmark template and share.
[15:38] Evan: timeline for bench run?
[15:40] Olivia: once we have samples, 48-72 hours to run and analyze; we can deliver a report with recommendations.
[15:48] Priya: any compliance docs we should see before Dedicated?
[15:51] Samir: we'll share SOC 2, ISO docs, and a security whitepaper for Dedicated / Private.
[15:58] Maya: thanks.
[16:02] [16:00] Jordan: quick dig into quantization: run your accuracy and latency delta per prompt set. sometimes 4-bit works great but for certain instruction-following prompts you might see regressions; we can run quality evals tied to your prompt set.
[16:19] Evan: we'll provide eval prompts as part of the sample.
[16:23] Olivia: good. another tip: for multi-model routing, route low-latency requests to smaller models and fall back to larger models for high-quality responses; Redwood can automate fallback policies.
[16:37] Maya: do fallbacks increase p99?
[16:39] Jordan: fallback adds routing overhead but keeps the system resilient; we recommend circuit breakers and quotas on fallback to prevent cascading latency.
[16:50] Evan: could you summarize quick wins vs medium-term changes?
[16:54] Olivia: quick wins (days): increase KV TTL for hot prefixes, reduce cross-AZ routing for critical routes, adjust retry policies, instrument first-byte. medium (weeks): adaptive batching, micro-chunk streaming, dedicated warm pools. longer (months): model quantization A/B and Dedicated capacity with denser GPUs.
[17:15] Samir: i'm going to recap at the end and list owners.
[17:18] [18:00] Maya: one more question on telemetry: we'd like token-level cost breakdowns — do you provide that?
[18:06] Samir: yes, Redwood Console gives token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route.
[18:11] Priya: for audit we need retention options.
[18:14] Samir: retention is configurable in Dedicated/Private; hosted has standard tiers.
[18:20] Evan: any gotchas for on-prem?
[18:23] Olivia: ops complexity and upgrade path — we provide tooling but you'll need infra engineers for air-gapped upgrades.
[18:31] Liam: acceptable.
[18:34] [19:00] Olivia: ok, let's run through a concrete test plan: Helio provides 24h anonymized sample, Redwood prepares a benchmark cluster that mimics traffic, run with current configs (4-bit, non-streaming), then run experiments toggling: micro-chunk streaming, adaptive batching, increased KV TTL, 8-bit quant, and AZ-local routing. we'll produce a report with p50/p95/p99 first-byte and completion times plus cost delta.
[19:27] Evan: sounds good.
[19:30] Samir: any blockers on Helio side?
[19:33] Maya: none, we'll scrub data and share.
[19:36] Priya: ensure legal signs off on the sample share.
[19:39] Samir: understood.
[19:43] [20:00] Jordan: i'll attach a benchmark template to the follow-up note.
[20:06] Olivia: and we'll add instrumentation suggestions for Datadog.
[20:10] Evan: timeline recap?
[20:12] Samir: Samir to send pricing & security docs by 2027-09-10; Olivia to send benchmark template & run script by 2027-09-14; Helio to share scrubbed 24h sample by 2027-09-12; Redwood to schedule benchmark kickoff for week of 2027-09-20.
[20:36] Maya: perfect.
[20:40] [21:00] Speaker 1: small background noise.
[21:06] Samir: any final questions?
[21:09] Evan: none here, thanks.
[21:11] Priya: thanks everyone.
[21:14] Samir: thanks all, we'll follow up with notes and action items.
[21:20] [22:00] Olivia: quick note — we'll instrument kernel types and attach logs in the report.
[22:07] Evan: appreciated.
[22:10] [23:00] Samir: meeting adjourned.

Summary: Deep dive into p95/p99 tail causes: KV cache misses, cold workers, batching stragglers, cross-AZ hops, and quantization-induced kernel differences. Agreed next steps to run benchmarks and share docs.

References shared: Redwood latency playbook (https://redwood.example.com/latency-playbook), Benchmark template (will be attached in follow-up), SOC2/ISO security whitepaper (link provided in follow-up).

End of transcript.
